about: AP® Biology concept dependency map (Phase 0). Topics are listed grouped by chapter: the eight units in CED order, then the two skills chapters. Course order is the unit topics in CED order with each skill or drill topic placed right after its "after" topic (several with the same anchor keep their listed order). Every concept names the topic that teaches it and the concepts it directly depends on; nothing may depend on a concept taught later unless the topic declares a preview box for it, backed by a circularDependencies entry. A concept's aliases are the words its topic owns for the glossary and the page check: not strict synonyms, but words taught there. Labels with a parenthetical qualifier ("base (chemistry)") mark words with two meanings and are skipped by the page check. When a short early version and a full later version share a word, the early version owns the plain word and lists the full treatment in fullIn. Unit and topic facts come from docs/apbio-ced-map.json (our own words); validated by scripts/lib/apbio-map.mjs.

bigIdeas.name: Evolution
bigIdeas.summary: Life changes over time through natural selection and other processes, and all organisms are linked by common ancestry.

bigIdeas.name: Energetics
bigIdeas.summary: Living systems take in and use energy and matter to grow, reproduce, and stay organized.

bigIdeas.name: Information Storage and Transmission
bigIdeas.summary: Living systems store, pass on, and respond to information, from DNA to cell signals.

bigIdeas.name: Systems Interactions
bigIdeas.summary: Biological systems at every level, from molecules to ecosystems, interact, and those interactions produce complex properties.

everydayWords.about: Common words a high-school student already roughly knows. They may be used in their everyday sense before the topic that teaches them; the page check skips them and the glossary gives each a hover definition linking to where it is taught. Technical terms of the same concept stay strict.

concepts.term: uniform width of the double helix
energy budget of endotherms and ectotherms

circularDependencies.problem: Elements of life (1.2) says which elements build proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates and lipids, and that sulfur is in some amino acids, before 1.3-1.7 teach those molecules.
circularDependencies.detail: One-line short versions of the four molecule families and of amino acid ("the building blocks of proteins"). The short versions own the plain words; 1.4-1.7 own the technical vocabulary.

circularDependencies.problem: ATP is named in 1.2 (phosphorus), in active transport and pumps (2.5, 2.6) and for mitochondria (2.1), but energy coupling is taught in 3.4.
circularDependencies.detail: "ATP is the molecule cells use to carry energy; it contains phosphate groups." ATP hydrolysis, ADP and coupling stay in 3.4.

circularDependencies.problem: Starch (1.4), chloroplasts and mitochondria (2.1) and metabolic rate (2.2) need photosynthesis and cellular respiration, which are 3.5 and 3.6.
circularDependencies.detail: Taught as the two halves of the matter cycle in 1.2: producers build sugar from carbon dioxide and water using light; cells break sugar down to release energy as ATP and return carbon dioxide. No mechanism.

circularDependencies.problem: Hydrolysis (1.3), cellulose digestion (1.4) and lysosomes (2.1) need enzymes; enzyme structure is 3.1.
circularDependencies.detail: "Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions such as hydrolysis." Active site, substrate and catalysis wait for Unit 3.

circularDependencies.problem: Phospholipid bilayers (1.5) and cholesterol are explained by their place in membranes before the plasma membrane topic (2.3).
circularDependencies.detail: "Cell membranes are phospholipid bilayers." The fluid mosaic model and membrane proteins stay in 2.3.

circularDependencies.problem: Cellulose (1.4) is the material of plant cell walls; cell walls are a 2.4 topic.
circularDependencies.detail: The wall as a rigid layer outside the membrane made of polysaccharides; its role against bursting stays in 2.4 and 2.7.

circularDependencies.problem: The CED puts nucleic acids in Unit 1, but DNA structure in detail, replication and gene expression are Unit 6, and Units 2-5 talk about DNA, genes and chromosomes throughout.
circularDependencies.detail: 1.6 teaches nucleotides, the backbone, 5'/3' ends, antiparallel strands, base pairing and that a gene is a stretch of DNA whose base order is information. Purines and pyrimidines, histones and genomes wait for 6.1.

circularDependencies.problem: Ribosomes, rough ER and the nucleus (2.1) need mRNA and "gene expression"; signaling responses (4.2) and the cell cycle (4.5) need chromosomes and gene expression; transcription and translation are 6.3-6.4.
circularDependencies.detail: One paragraph in 2.1: DNA in the nucleus is packed into chromosomes; a gene's instructions are copied into messenger RNA, which ribosomes read to build a protein ("gene expression"). The words transcription and translation are not used until Unit 6.

circularDependencies.problem: Lysosomes help in programmed cell death (2.1), and a signaling response can be cell death (4.2); apoptosis is taught with the cell cycle (4.6).
circularDependencies.detail: "Apoptosis is a cell's orderly self-destruction." Triggers and caspases are in 4.6.

circularDependencies.problem: Membrane proteins receive signals (2.3), receptor-mediated endocytosis (2.5) and gated channels (2.6) need receptors and signaling molecules before Unit 4.
circularDependencies.detail: A receptor is a protein that a particular signaling molecule binds, changing the cell's behavior. Ligand, transduction and second messengers wait for Unit 4.

circularDependencies.problem: The sodium-potassium pump (2.6), proton gradients in chloroplasts and mitochondria (3.5, 3.6) and synaptic signaling (4.1) need a charge difference across a membrane; no CED topic teaches nerve impulses.
circularDependencies.detail: Taught with the pump: uneven ion distribution makes the inside of the cell negative, which stores energy like a battery. The proton-motive force in 3.5 builds on it.

circularDependencies.problem: Endosymbiosis (2.10), the origin of photosynthesis (3.5), shared genetic mechanisms (5.3) and the universal code (6.4) use evolution and common ancestry before Unit 7.
circularDependencies.detail: In 2.10: evolution is change in the inherited traits of populations over generations; shared features point to a common ancestor. Natural selection itself waits for 7.1 (see the mutations preview).

circularDependencies.problem: S phase copies DNA (4.5) two units before replication (6.2).
circularDependencies.detail: "Base pairing lets each strand serve as a pattern for a new partner strand." Enzymes and strand direction stay in 6.2.

circularDependencies.problem: Signal pathways can be stuck on by a mutation (4.3) and cell-cycle genes mutate in cancer (4.6) before mutations (6.7).
circularDependencies.detail: "A mutation is a change in a gene's DNA sequence, which can change the protein." Mutation types, frameshifts and causes stay in 6.7.

circularDependencies.problem: Homologous chromosomes (5.1) and crossing over (5.2) carry different alleles before Mendelian genetics (5.3).
circularDependencies.detail: "Alleles are different versions of the same gene." Dominance, genotype and phenotype stay in 5.3.

circularDependencies.problem: The CED lists phospholipids among the molecules that need phosphorus (1.2); phospholipids are 1.5.
circularDependencies.detail: Preview box: "phospholipids, the fats that make up cell membranes, contain a phosphate group." Not worth a pull-forward: nothing else in 1.2-1.4 needs it.

circularDependencies.problem: Whether a mutation is harmful, neutral or helpful depends on the environment through natural selection (6.7), taught in 7.1.
circularDependencies.detail: Preview box: individuals whose variants suit the environment leave more offspring, so a variant's value depends on where the organism lives.

circularDependencies.problem: K-selected life histories (8.3) are defined against carrying capacity, taught in 8.4.
circularDependencies.detail: Preview box: "the largest population an environment can support over time (K)".

circularDependencies.problem: Predation is a standard density-dependent factor (8.4), but predation is taught with community interactions (8.5).
circularDependencies.detail: Preview box: predators eat prey, and catch more when prey are crowded. "Predator" and "prey" are also everyday words.
